files.lesson.md: --- order: 18 unit: quad9 node: AC9M9A04 n1 uses: [AC9M7A05 n3] assumes: [AC9M7A05 n3] connection: handshakes title: Recognising a quadratic summary: "A table is quadratic when its second differences are constant: the first differences change, but by the same amount each time." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Everyone in a group shakes hands with everyone else once. How many handshakes for 6 people? Does the count go up at a steady rate?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8365 url: http://127.0.0.1:8365/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- Some patterns grow at a steady rate, and those make straight lines. Others grow faster each time. One kind of speeding-up pattern is called quadratic. ## Predict: more people, more handshakes ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the next number in a handshake count shows who keeps adding the same amount and who spots that each step adds more." check: type: predict q: "In a group, everyone shakes hands with everyone else once. 2 people make 1 handshake, 3 make 3, 4 make 6 and 5 make 10. How many handshakes for 6 people?" options: - "15" - "13" - "14" - "12" actual: "15. The count goes up by 2, then 3, then 4. The next step goes up by 5, so 10 + 5 = 15. A new person shakes hands with everyone already there, so each person adds one more handshake than the last." ``` The count goes 1, 3, 6, 10. What comes next? ## Run: read the handshakes ```step stage: run insight: "Sliding along the graph of handshake counts shows each count and how the climb gets steeper, which is how a quadratic differs from a straight line." try: { playground: board, starter: "recognise.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Slide the cursor to 6 people. How many handshakes? Was your prediction right?", when: "x(R) = 6" } ``` The dots show the handshakes for each group size. Slide the cursor along and watch how the count climbs. ## Investigate: differences ```step stage: investigate insight: "Subtract each value from the next to get the first differences. If those change by the same amount each time, the second differences are constant and the table is quadratic." tasks: - check: type: number q: "The handshake counts for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 people are $0, 1, 3, 6, 10$. The first differences are $1, 2, 3, 4$. What is the second difference (the change in the first differences)?" answer: 1 explain: "1, 2, 3, 4 goes up by 1 each time, so the second difference is 1." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "From $1, 2, 3, 4$, how much does each number go up by?", answer: 1, explain: "2 − 1 = 1, 3 − 2 = 1 and 4 − 3 = 1." } - check: type: question q: "Which table of $y$ values (for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$) is quadratic?" options: ["$3, 6, 11, 18$", "$3, 6, 9, 12$", "$3, 6, 12, 24$", "$3, 7, 11, 15$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The first differences are all 3: that's a straight line.", "The first differences are 3, 6, 12. They double, so the second differences (3, 6) aren't equal.", "The first differences are all 4: that's a straight line."] explain: "3, 6, 11, 18 has first differences 3, 5, 7 and constant second differences 2, 2." - check: type: question q: "Which equation gives a quadratic relationship?" options: ["$y = x^2 - 4$", "$y = 3x + 2$", "$y = \\dfrac{5}{x}$", "$y = 2x - x$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That's a straight line: x only to the power 1.", "x is on the bottom: that's a different kind of curve.", "2x − x is just x: a straight line."] explain: "A quadratic has $x^2$ as its highest power." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#sam" text: "Sam looks at the table $y = 2, 5, 10, 17$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: quadratic-needs-equal-first-differences explain: "Line 3: unequal first differences don't rule out a quadratic. Equal first differences mean a straight line. A quadratic has equal second differences: 2, 2." ``` ### Second differences Here's testing a table. ```worked y = 3, 6, 11, 18, 27 :: The table for x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. \text{first differences: } 3, 5, 7, 9 :: Subtract each value from the next. \text{second differences: } 2, 2, 2 :: Subtract again. \text{constant, so the table is quadratic} :: The second differences are all equal. ``` Now try one on paper: $y = 0, 2, 8, 18, 32$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. Work out the first differences, then type the second difference. ### Which table? ### Which equation? ### Find the mistake Read Sam's working. Which line draws the wrong conclusion? ## Modify: change the numbers ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing a changes the second difference: for y = ax², it is 2a. And a = 0 is no quadratic at all." try: { playground: board, starter: "recognise.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - hint: ["Try a = 2 first and read the table.", "The values for a = 3 are 0, 3, 12, 27, …"] check: { type: board, text: "Set $a$ so the table starts $0, 3, 12, 27$.", when: "a = 3" } - hint: ["For y = ax², the second difference is 2a.", "2a = 6."] check: { type: number, q: "A table has constant second differences of 6 and follows $y = ax^2$. What is $a$?", answer: 3, explain: "The second difference is 2a, so 2a = 6 and a = 3." } - hint: ["Set a = 0 on the board.", "Look at the table."] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: $a = 0$ so $y = 0x^2$. Is it a quadratic?", options: ["No: every value is 0, so there's no curve", "Yes: it still has an x²", "Yes: it's a quadratic with a flat curve", "It depends on x"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "0 times x² is 0, so the x² has gone.", "A quadratic needs a curve.", "The values are 0 for every x."], explain: "With a = 0, y is always 0: a flat line, not a quadratic. A quadratic needs a not 0." } ``` ### Find a ### Second difference to a ### When a is 0 ## Practise: quadratic or not? ```step stage: practise insight: "Differences on a table decide: equal first differences are linear, equal second differences are quadratic. Then you can extend the pattern." tasks: - check: type: number q: "For $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ a table gives $y = 1, 2, 5, 10, 17$. What is the second difference?" answer: 2 explain: "First differences 1, 3, 5, 7. Second differences 2, 2, 2." - check: type: question q: "A table gives $y = 4, 7, 10, 13$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$. What kind of relationship is it?" options: ["Linear: the first differences are all 3", "Quadratic: it keeps going up", "Neither", "You can't tell from four values"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Going up isn't enough: a quadratic has changing first differences.", "Equal first differences make a straight line.", "Four values are enough to see equal differences."] explain: "7 − 4 = 3, 10 − 7 = 3, 13 − 10 = 3: linear." - check: type: number q: "A quadratic table has $y = 3, 5, 9, 15$. The second differences are 2. What is the next $y$ value?" answer: 23 explain: "First differences 2, 4, 6. The next is 8, so the next value is 15 + 8 = 23." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "The first differences are $2, 4, 6$. What is the next first difference?", answer: 8, explain: "They go up by 2 each time." } - check: type: number q: "Review: what is the gradient of the line through $(1, 3)$ and $(3, 9)$?" answer: 3 explain: "Rise 6, run 2: 6 ÷ 2 = 3." ``` ### The second difference ### Linear or quadratic ### The next value ### Review From the first unit: rise over run. ## Make: more handshakes ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the handshakes: extend the pattern with differences, and check what the count means for a bigger group." tasks: - hint: ["Write the differences: 1, 2, 3, 4, …", "Keep adding the next difference."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The handshake counts for 2, 3, 4, 5 people are $1, 3, 6, 10$. Extend the table to find the count for 8 people." steps: - ["$\\text{first differences: } 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$", "each new person adds one more handshake than the last"] - ["$10 + 5 = 15, 15 + 6 = 21, 21 + 7 = 28$", "keep adding the next difference"] - ["28 handshakes", "for 8 people"] answer: "28" answerLabel: "Handshakes for 8 people" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["24", "That adds 5 each time. The amount added goes up by 1 each time."] - ["21", "That's the count for 7 people. Add one more difference."] criteria: - "I wrote the first differences and saw them go up by 1." - "I carried the pattern on from 10 for each extra person." - "I counted people carefully: 8 people, not 8 handshakes." explain: "5, 6, 7 added to 10 gives 15, 21, 28. So 8 people make 28 handshakes." - check: type: number q: "How many handshakes for 10 people?" answer: 45 explain: "28 + 8 = 36 for 9 people, and 36 + 9 = 45 for 10." ``` ### Eight people Back to the handshakes. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Ten people The group sizes here are a pattern to work with, not a measurement. **Also used in** - **Networks.** If every computer in a network is linked directly to every other, the number of links grows the same way. - **Sport.** A round-robin competition with $n$ teams needs the same number of matches. - **Next lesson.** Drawing a quadratic: the curve, its highest point and where it crosses the axes. ```teacher summary: Students recognise a quadratic from the constant second differences of a table or from an x² in the equation (AC9M9A04, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can find first and second differences of a table. - I can tell a linear table from a quadratic one. - I can use the second differences to carry on a quadratic pattern. struggle: "Stopping at the first differences. Ask: are the first differences equal? If not, what do you do next?" before: > Students need Plotting a rule from Year 7. The one idea: equal first differences make a line, and equal second differences make a quadratic. The common mistake is stopping when the first differences aren't equal (Sam's working). The handshake counts are a number pattern. Nothing here is a measurement. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 13 or 14 kept adding 3 or 4, as if the pattern were steady." - "Run: ask students to say how much each new person adds." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the 8 people in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for a row of first differences." - "Modify: before the second task, ask what the second difference is for a = 1 and a = 2." stuck: - see: A student says a table isn't quadratic because the first differences aren't equal. ask: What happens if you take the differences again? fix: Equal second differences make it quadratic. - see: A student thinks y = 3x + 2 is quadratic because it goes up. ask: What power of x is there? fix: "Only x to the power 1: a straight line." stretch: Show that the second difference of y = ax² is always 2a. support: A printed table with empty rows for the first and second differences. leads: > Continues AC9M9A04 node 1. Where it leads: graphing a quadratic next, and modelling stopping distances later in the unit. exit: q: A table gives y = 2, 6, 12, 20 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Linear, quadratic or neither? a: "Quadratic: first differences 4, 6, 8, second differences 2, 2." explain: > A table is linear when its first differences are equal. It is quadratic when its first differences change by the same amount each time, so its second differences are equal. A quadratic equation has x² as its highest power. ```
files.recognise.yml:
# Boards for "Recognising a quadratic". Handshake counts, then y = ax² with its table.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: 0, 9
y: -2, 40
grid: 1, 5
axes: People, Handshakes
snap: 1
series Handshakes: 1,0; 2,1; 3,3; 4,6; 5,10; 6,15; 7,21; 8,28
cursor R: 2
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -2, 90
grid: 1, 10
slider a: 0, 3, 1, 1
plot: y = ax^2, from 0
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
# endregion
